description: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts by systematically guessing passwords. This specific profile identifies brute-forcing directed at the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) service, characterized by automated, rapid, and repetitive authentication attempts.

patterns.description: Behaviors specific to the FTP command structure during the authentication phase.

features.name: Repetitive USER/PASS Cycles
features.description: The traffic consists almost entirely of FTP 'USER' and 'PASS' commands followed by server rejection responses (typically FTP response code 530 Not logged in), with no actual file transfer data (LIST, RETR, STOR) occurring.

features.name: Small Packet/Payload Constraints
features.description: Because the connections only consist of short text-based usernames and passwords, the average packet length remains distinctly small and uniform throughout the flow.

patterns.description: Anomalies indicating an automated script is driving the connection attempts rather than a human user.

features.name: High Forward Packet Rate (Connection Thrashing)
features.description: A significantly high rate of forward packets (High Fwd Pkts/s and High Flow Pkts/s) directed exclusively at the FTP control port (TCP 21), indicating aggressive connection initiation.

features.name: Symmetrical/Balanced Flow Ratio
features.description: Unlike DoS attacks, brute force attempts usually complete the TCP handshake and receive a server response for every guess. This creates a relatively balanced ratio of Forward to Backward packets, even at high speeds.

patterns.description: Metrics highlighting the automated teardown of failed sessions.

features.name: Micro-Session Durations
features.description: Because the FTP server immediately drops the connection or the client tears it down after a failed guess, the overall lifespan of each individual network flow (Low Flow Duration) is extremely short.

features.name: Machine-Speed Inter-Arrival Time
features.description: The mean time between packets and between consecutive connections (Low Flow IAT Mean) is minimal, reflecting an automated script instantly firing the next guess rather than a human typing.

patterns.description: Indicators to separate malicious password guessing from benign operational errors.

features.name: Sequential or Dictionary Sequencing
features.description: Deep packet inspection may reveal usernames being tested alphabetically or passwords being pulled predictably from common dictionary lists.

features.name: Misconfigured Automation (False Positive Filtering)
features.description: Rapid bursts of failed FTP logins can often be triggered by benign but broken automated systems, such as a nightly backup script using expired credentials or an improperly configured automated web deployment tool.
